'''Walter C. Oechel''' (born January 15, 1945) is a researcher who studies the areas of plant eco-physiology, systems ecology, global change, and biosphere-atmosphere interaction.<ref name=Metro /> At [[San Diego State University]] he is as a Distinguished Professor of Biology,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kpbs.org/news/2007/mar/21/global-warming-effects-here-now/|title=Global Warming Effects Here Now|first=Ed|last=Joyce|date=21 March 2007 }}</ref> as well as at the [[Open University]], UK.<ref name=Price>{{cite web|url=http://newscenter.sdsu.edu/sdsu_newscenter/news_story.aspx?sid=75962|title=NewsCenter - SDSU - Methane Emissions in Arctic Cold Season Higher Than Expected}}</ref> He is also co-director of the Center for Climate and [[Sustainability studies|Sustainability Studies]] (C2S2) and  the director of the Global Change Research Group at SDSU.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/WNT/Science/story?id=1164442&page=1|title=Troubling Signs of Climate Change Seen in Arctic|publisher=ABC News|date=7 January 2006}}</ref>

== Research ==
Oechel has published over 250 papers and his H index is 71. His journal papers have been cited more than 22,000 times. He started his research in eco-physiology with Boyd Strain and WD Billings and moved on to ecosystem studies, global change research, and biosphere-atmosphere interaction. He discovered loss of CO<sub>2</sub> from Arctic ecosystems due to global warming<ref>Oechel et al. 1993 and 2000, Nature</ref> and limits to CO<sub>2</sub> fertilization effects in the Arctic.<ref>Oechel et al. 1994, Nature</ref> With NSF funding, he developed the first university owned and operated EC [[flux]] aircraft anywhere in the world, the Sky Arrow 650TCN Environmental Research Aircraft for CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O, energy and latter CH<sub>4</sub>.

During the 1980s, Oechel led a team studying [[global warming]] at [[Toolik Lake]] and [[Barrow, Alaska]] to measure the greenhouse gases emitted by high Arctic vegetation, where they found evidence that the ground was emitting more gases than it was absorbing, changing the previous understanding of how the Arctic works in the global climate system.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://science.sciencemag.org/content/304/5677/news-summaries|title=News this Week|first=American Association for the Advancement of|last=Science|date=11 June 2004|volume=304|issue=5677|pages=1576|via=science.sciencemag.org}}</ref>

In 2009 he released a further study showing that wetlands developing in Alaska emitted even more greenhouse gases than the previously frozen tundra.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.nature.com/news/2009/090804/full/news.2009.778.html|title=Drowned tundra emits more carbon|journal=Nature|first=Alexandra|last=Witze|date=4 August 2009|via=www.nature.com|doi=10.1038/news.2009.778|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Part of the principle behind these studies is that the Arctic ice had been pulling carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere over the millennia, which was released as ice melted due to global warming.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QJQkw1EsxcEC&pg=PA19|title=Once and Future Giants: What Ice Age Extinctions Tell Us About the Fate of Earth's Largest Animals|first=Sharon|last=Levy|date=22 March 2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|via=Google Books|isbn=9780199831548}}</ref> He has also shown that the world's oceans add more to the total greenhouse gas emissions than human activity does, adding substantially to global warming issues.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vaTALb2I5KoC&pg=PT393|title=The Whale and the Supercomputer: On the Northern Front of Climate Change|first=Charles|last=Wohlforth|date=4 May 2005|publisher=Macmillan|via=Google Books|isbn=9781429923743}}</ref>
The [[National Science Foundation]] in 2004 wrote that, 
<br />
<blockquote> Oechel's extensive work on CO<sub>2</sub> on every continent except Antarctica has had important implications for understanding global warming. His efforts impact virtually every aspect of research on climate change and ecosystems science. His use of cutting-edge technology has provided near real-time ecophysiological data on the Web for many K-20 classrooms, and he has developed K-12 interactive science education among United States and Mexico border schools.<ref name=NSF /> </blockquote>
That year he was named a Distinguished Teaching Scholar by the National Science Foundation, receiving the Director's Award for Distinguished Teaching Scholars, NSF's highest award for combinative teaching and research excellence.<ref name=NSF>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=100387&org=NSF&from=news|title=NSF Names Eight Distinguished Teaching Scholars - NSF - National Science Foundation}}</ref> Later, Oechel and Donatella Zona coinvented an on-demand heating system for atmospheric measuring towers in order for Arctic scientists to take measurements year-round.<ref name=Price />

This system allowed the discovery of large fall emissions in methane loss from the Arctic, especially during the fall "Zero Curtain" period.  It also allowed the discovery that upland, non-inundated tundra can be a more active emitter of methane than wet, inundated areas changing the perception of the importance of the cold season and upland tundra on annual methane emission balances. Oechel has studied the importance of marine coastal and riverine systems on the global C balance in Arctic, temperate, and tropical regions.

In 2014, Oechel was named one of the "World's Most Influential Scientific Minds", rated by Thomson Reuters, topping the "agricultural sciences" category.<ref name=Metro>{{cite web|url=http://www.sandiegometro.com/2014/07/daily-business-report-july-16-2014/|title=Daily Business Report — July 16, 2014, San Diego Metro Magazine|date=16 July 2014}}</ref> In 2015, Oechel co-developed a study with Harvard, [[NASA]], and other institutions that showed methane was also being released into the atmosphere during the winter months from the ground of the Arctic than previously believed, increased the amount of presumed greenhouse gases released globally per year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kpbs.org/news/2015/dec/21/san-diego-state-study-could-change-global-climate-/|title=San Diego State Study Could Change Global Climate Models|first=City News|last=Service|date=21 December 2015 }}</ref>

Oechel has appeared on national news shows discussing the problem of climate change, such as, ABC News<ref>{{cite web|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=1765362&page=1|title=Is It Too Late to Stop the Warming?|publisher=ABC News|date=27 March 2006}}</ref> and The Washington Post.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/energy-environment/wp/2015/12/21/bad-news-scientists-say-we-could-be-underestimating-arctic-methane-emissions/|title=Bad news: Scientists say we could be underestimating Arctic methane emissions|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] }}</ref>
